gist: Bloomberg Intelligence ETF analysts Eric Balchunas and James Seyffart join The Compound & Friends during a violent AI-trade crash (SanDisk halved in 17 days, CoreWeave -77%, tech P/E down 43% even as EPS rose 76%) and Jensen Huang's surprise return as Nvidia CEO. They argue leveraged-ETF traders are disciplined dip-buyers, that SPY's $100B-volume day marked a 'code red', that HALO and garbage stocks are the anti-AI hedge, and that daily active-ETF disclosure (their 'Blue Horseshoe' signal) shows smart money in real time. Their Bitcoin book, published into a 70% drawdown, sees money printing or price momentum as the next catalyst.

themes.theme: Jensen Huang reinstatement and Nvidia politics

insights.claim: Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, announced around 9am Monday before the open, shocked the panel: hosts had put the odds of a return before year-end at roughly 5% (10-20 to one), James Seyffart expected weeks at minimum, and Eric Balchunas put it at 20%, rising to 50% if the stock fell below $100.
insights.speaker: hosts and guests
insights.so_what: Shows how badly consensus underestimated a board's willingness to reverse a CEO ouster when the stock is collapsing; the stock price itself was a lever for the return.
insights.quote: I would have put the odds way lower. Like I I thought he was definitely gone for at least a lot longer time.

insights.claim: Eric Balchunas's base case had been that an ousted Jensen would eventually take a job at, or start, another semiconductor company that Nvidia would then acquire, a roughly 18-month path with a lot of stock damage along the way.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: A founder-CEO's departure often doesn't end his economic link to the franchise; watch for acqui-hire paths after leadership shocks.
insights.quote: I thought he would ultimately take a job at another semiconductor company or start one and then Nvidia would acquire it.

insights.claim: The return became possible because subsequent reporting (New York Times, Wall Street Journal) backed off any clear link between Jensen's affair and chip-smuggling espionage, turning a national-security issue into a personal-conduct issue.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: How a scandal is classified (personal vs. national security) decides whether a CEO can come back; watch for the framing to shift.
insights.quote: if he comes back it becomes a matter of like well he was unfaithful but that's a personal issue versus a national security issue.

insights.claim: The panel frames the reinstatement as 'winning cures': a CEO who drives the stock up gets privileges others don't (compared to Deshaun Watson and Bobby Knight), so the more value a CEO creates, the more conduct boards will tolerate.
insights.speaker: hosts
insights.so_what: Key-person risk at mega-cap founder-led companies is lopsided: governance discipline weakens the more the market depends on the person.
insights.quote: So everyone's equal but some people are more equal than others.

insights.claim: The US government's 15% cut of Nvidia's allowed China chip sales got little attention over the prior months, even though it ties the administration's interests directly to Nvidia's revenue.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: The government's revenue share helps explain the White House's support for Jensen and is a policy channel to watch for Nvidia's China sales.
insights.quote: The government has a 15% rake on the uh chips that they're able to sell.

insights.claim: A theory going around holds that Anthropic and OpenAI leadership wanted Jensen out because he was Washington's loudest advocate for open-weight models, including enabling Chinese competitors. Views on his return split cleanly along political lines, matching an AI 'civil war' over open versus gated models.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Open-weight vs. closed-model policy has become partisan; regulation outcomes could shift economics between chip vendors and frontier labs.
insights.quote: Jensen came out very forcefully for openweight models >> and was the leading advocate in Washington for why we should also enable Chinese uh who are building competitive models.

insights.claim: The Nvidia story combines sex, politics, China, tech, AI and Trump, so the panel expects it to stay a top story for a while, unlike most news cycles, with the stock still volatile and falling sharply on recording day.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Expect continued headline-driven volatility in Nvidia and the stocks tied to it rather than a quick fade.
insights.quote: it's got everything. You know that this is a >> right >> sex, it's politics, it's China, it's tech, it's AI, it's Trump, it's like literally it's an everything story.

insights.claim: The Friday SEC-probe headline on Nvidia set off the biggest single-stock selling day of the year by Robinhood traders, who dumped Nvidia into the close.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Retail capitulation in single stocks (as some rotated into ETFs) is a sentiment marker near local lows.

themes.theme: AI trade crash and multiple compression

insights.claim: The AI-trade drawdowns are severe: SanDisk fell from about $140 to below $70 in 17 trading days, CoreWeave is down 77% and below its $40 IPO price, Nebius is down 70%, Oracle 68%, Western Digital 65%, Dell and Micron 50%, Broadcom 40%, AMD 37%, and Nvidia 30% after having been down 47%.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Memory, neocloud and AI-infrastructure names have already priced a lot of the bust; this sets the reference levels for any rebound or further capitulation.
insights.quote: The stock got cut in half in less than a month in like 17 trading days.

insights.claim: Leveraged and themed products have spread to private AI names, with 14 Anthropic leveraged and covered-call ETFs already in existence. The neocloud ETF was called 'perfectly designed to be bet against' in this kind of market.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: A rush of leveraged and covered-call wrappers on a hot theme is a froth signal; narrow thematic ETFs can work as short vehicles.
insights.quote: There is 14 anthropic leverage ETFs and covered call ETFs already.

insights.claim: Technology-sector EPS is up 76% this year while its P/E has fallen 43%, so the selloff is entirely multiple compression with earnings estimates still rising. Every sector except consumer staples has seen its P/E fall year to date.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Earnings support is intact; if growth holds, compressed multiples set up a re-rating, and the risk lies in sentiment rather than fundamentals.
insights.quote: technology EPS is up 76% this year. The PE is down 43%. How crazy is that?

insights.claim: After Nasdaq returns of 55% (2023), 26% (2024) and 21% (2025), the market may have priced the earnings in advance. Repeated 20-30% years destabilize investors, so any catalyst triggers a selloff, and investors used to automatic gains sell in despondency when they stop.
insights.speaker: hosts
insights.so_what: Expect a breather year after a run of big up years even with strong earnings; pricing ahead of profits limits near-term upside.
insights.quote: That's the destabilizing force is just having them be up so much.

insights.claim: Semiconductors reached 19% of the S&P 500, an industry-group weight that has historically never ended well. The panel dubbed this the 'Icarus rule' of flying too close to the sun.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Use extreme index weight in a single industry group as a warning sign of concentration risk and a cue to trim or hedge.
insights.quote: The semis were 19% of the S&P. That never goes well after for any sector that becomes that large a part of the market.

insights.claim: Tony Kim, who runs BlackRock's AI and tech ETF (BAI), thinks the market is pricing an AI plateau next year followed by a decline.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: If an AI plateau is the consensus, an AI capex surprise next year could catch the market leaning the wrong way.
insights.quote: He said that he thinks the market is pricing a sort of plateau of AI next year and then it's going to go down.

insights.claim: Eric Balchunas's framework: as long as earnings hold up, selloffs are noise. If earnings take a big hit, it means a real-world shock (like COVID) is under way, and the government will then step in, so he doesn't worry much about the stock market.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Watch earnings revisions rather than price; a falling-earnings scenario likely brings fiscal or monetary support.
insights.quote: So, as long as earnings are up, I think don't worry about the stock market.

insights.claim: After the correction, the S&P 500's P/E is around 20, about its 25-year average, and roughly 16 times forward earnings.
insights.speaker: hosts and guests
insights.so_what: Valuation is no longer stretched at the index level, which supports buying the correction if earnings hold.

insights.claim: According to Willie Delwiche, the market has had 60 straight days of more new lows than new highs, the second-longest such stretch in a decade, behind only the 71-day run at the end of 2008.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Internal breadth damage is historically extreme even with the index's drawdown modest; it marks either capitulation or deeper trouble.
insights.quote: only the 71 days in row of more new lows than new highs at the end of 2008 lasted longer than the current 60 days in a row.

insights.claim: Equal-weight versus cap-weight (RSP divided by SPY) is breaking out to its highest level in a long time, so the average stock is holding up while the mega-cap AI leaders fall.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Rotation into equal-weight and non-AI stocks is under way; equal-weight exposure diversifies away from AI concentration.
insights.quote: RSP divided by SPY is breaking out. It's It's at the highest levels in a long time.

insights.claim: Waste Management and Republic Services are the two S&P 500 stocks most inversely correlated to DRAM, and Waste Management just hit an all-time high in the middle of the AI selloff.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Garbage haulers act as an anti-AI or anti-memory hedge for portfolios heavy in the AI trade.
insights.quote: Those are the two most inversely correlated stocks to DRAM

themes.theme: HALO vs AI ETFs and product naming

insights.claim: The host's 'HALO' theme (heavy assets, low obsolescence), an equal-weighted ETF holding names like Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Masco, Constellation Brands, Lowe's, Domino's and Waste Management, is outperforming BlackRock's AI and tech active ETF (BAI), which is down 40% this year.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Physical-asset businesses that AI can't easily make obsolete are the winning theme of the AI unwind and a candidate hedge for AI-heavy portfolios.
insights.quote: Literally versus the Eyesshares AI and tech active ETF. I'm outperforming him.

insights.claim: Despite the performance gap, BAI holds $10.7 billion while the HALO ETF has $36 million, which Eric Balchunas credits to distribution (BlackRock versus Round Hill) and retail appetite for exciting themes. He expects the defensive theme to get no love until the end of a bear market.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Asset flows follow distribution and narrative, not performance; small defensive thematic funds tend to attract assets only late in a downturn.
insights.quote: distribution is king, man.

insights.claim: Product naming drives flows: covered-call strategies did nothing until JPMorgan rebranded them 'equity premium income'. Eric argues the HALO theme needs an edgier, simpler name, because theme ETFs are almost 100% bought by retail and advisers don't buy them.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: For ETF issuers and flow-watchers, branding is a leading indicator of which strategies will gather assets.
insights.quote: Cover call didn't do anything until JP Morgan called it equity premium income.

themes.theme: Leveraged ETF flows and retail behavior

insights.claim: In the week that included the worst selloff Friday, the top ETF inflows were VOO first, then the triple-levered semiconductor ETF SOXL (about $3 billion) and VTI, with some money going to cash. 'Vanguardians' buy no matter what, alongside dip-buying 'degens' in SOXL and TQQQ.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Retail dip-buying into leveraged semis shows no capitulation among retail; long-term index buyers provide steady support.
insights.quote: Three billion into a triple levered semiconductor ETF.

insights.claim: SOXL's daily moves show how violent the market has become: down 24% that morning, down 24% the day before, up 40% Monday (another speaker said up 64%) after a 32% drop the prior day, and roughly 70% off the morning lows by 2pm on recording day.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Daily-reset leveraged semis are trading like lottery tickets; volatility decay makes holding them long-term costly.
insights.quote: These are the daily returns of Soxall. So today, this morning it was down 24%. Yesterday it fell 24%.

insights.claim: Contrary to the 'dumb money' stereotype, leveraged-ETF traders fade the market by selling into rallies and buying dips. SOXL and TQQQ trade daily volume comparable to Amazon and have lifetime outflows despite returns of about 10,000%, which implies roughly $25 billion of wealth created ($16 billion in assets plus $11 billion taken out).
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Leveraged-ETF flows are contrarian and act as liquidity providers on dips; flow data from them shouldn't be read as momentum chasing.
insights.quote: They're using them as an ATM machine because generally this trade has gone up

insights.claim: SPY dollar volume above $100 billion marks a 'code red' crisis day, which has happened roughly 10 times ever; $60 billion is the 'freakout zone'. The latest Friday topped $100 billion, and QQQ and SOXL volumes were near top-three days ever.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Use SPY volume thresholds as a capitulation gauge; $100B+ days historically line up with crisis extremes.
insights.quote: 60 billion is the freakout zone.

insights.claim: The top 20 leveraged ETFs lost $81 billion in assets very quickly. These are asset losses net of new money, since dip buyers kept adding even as prices collapsed.
insights.speaker: host and James Seyffart
insights.so_what: Shows how much retail capital the daily-reset products destroy in a fast drawdown, even though flows were positive.
insights.quote: this is the top 20 leverage ETFs losing $81 billion in assets

insights.claim: Leveraged ETFs and their options are amplifying market moves through self-referential rebalancing, especially around the close, and options open interest on leveraged single-stock ETFs has 'gone supercharged since 2025'.
insights.speaker: James Seyffart
insights.so_what: End-of-day rebalancing flows from leveraged products can exaggerate closing moves; expect stocks with large leveraged-ETF footprints to overshoot.
insights.quote: They're amplifiers of what's going on in moose particularly around the close

insights.claim: The SEC is drawing a line: existing 3x products are grandfathered, but new 3x, 4x and 5x filings won't be approved. A 5x Nasdaq ETF exists in Europe but gets no demand, and Athanasios's study found 3x single-stock ETFs on volatile names like quantum stocks would hit termination events (a 33% underlying drop) every week or two.
insights.speaker: James Seyffart
insights.so_what: Expect no escalation in leverage at the product level, which caps the growth of the most extreme products; regulatory limits shape where speculative flows go.
insights.quote: The line is new 3x is not going to happen.

insights.claim: Single-stock leveraged ETFs found real demand, with the 2x long Nvidia ETF exceeding $6 billion at one point. Index-level leveraged products are traded more than their underlying assets, while smaller single-stock versions trade less than expected.
insights.speaker: James Seyffart
insights.so_what: Single-stock leverage is now a meaningful flow source in mega-caps like Nvidia.

insights.claim: SOXL is the most traded ETF in Korea, where retail investors who were long barred from other gambling discovered leveraged SK Hynix and semiconductor products. Korean retail, like US retail, splits between a vanilla retirement account and a speculative 'cowboy account'.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Korean retail is a large marginal buyer of leveraged US semis and memory names, so their sentiment feeds back into SOXL and SK Hynix moves.
insights.quote: Soxel is the number one most traded ETF in Korea.

themes.theme: ETF industry economics and product proliferation

insights.claim: The 'Jack Bogle paradox': ETFs charging 0-10 bps make up 58% of assets but only 16% of revenue. The more money flows to cheap vanilla funds, the crazier the new launches, because one expensive hit product makes an issuer 'set for life', like a lottery ticket.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Expect continued proliferation of high-fee niche, leveraged and themed products; issuer economics depend on them, not on index funds.
insights.quote: They make up 58% of the assets but only 16% of the revenue.

insights.claim: Roughly one new ETF launches for every $1 billion of daily ETF inflows, about 1,400 launches a year (about 110 a month). The average ETF holds $3 billion but the median only about $10 million, and launch costs have fallen so much that the 'spaghetti cannon' approach of throwing products at the market works.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Launch counts track inflows; a slowdown in launches would signal weakening flows.

insights.claim: Sports-team ETFs (NBA and hockey) are coming: an index of about 50 team components scored on game results, CME futures trading off the index, and ETFs tracking the futures. They are pitched as an uncorrelated return stream or a hedge for team owners. A host called them a sign that 'capitalism has gone too far', while Eric argued the market will decide.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas and host
insights.so_what: A product-cycle froth marker; there is no investment case beyond novelty, and the hosts expect little money to go in.
insights.quote: Capitalism has gone too far.

insights.claim: Bloomberg Intelligence uses a traffic-light rating in which leveraged or futures-rolling products get a red light, like an R-rated movie. Eric wants it distributed to brokerages as a surgeon-general-style warning, and says the bigger crime is a product that doesn't deliver what it promises, such as a 3x fund that returns 1.5x.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Expect more product disclosure friction at brokerages rather than bans; tracking accuracy is the key due-diligence test for leveraged products.

insights.claim: A host argued that issuers ask not what investors need but what they will buy, and that commentators have a duty to warn retail that they are being studied like 'a chimpanzee in a cage'. Guests countered that 90%+ of industry assets sit in sensible products and that leveraged ETFs lose money slower than a casino or a sports bet.
insights.speaker: host vs. Eric Balchunas and James Seyffart
insights.so_what: Retail-protection backlash against speculative products is a growing regulatory and reputational risk for issuers and brokerages.
insights.quote: They're asking themselves, "What will these motheruckers buy?"

insights.claim: Active ETFs, now about $2 trillion and increasingly run by the same managers as Capital Group and Fidelity mutual funds, publish their holdings every day. For the first time, investors can see 'big active' fund managers' trades daily instead of 45-90 days after the quarter ends.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Daily disclosure creates a new real-time data source on institutional positioning.
insights.quote: Because active ETFs show their holdings every day and they have two trillion

insights.claim: Bloomberg Intelligence's 'Blue Horseshoe' indicator (sorted by BH in the terminal's ETF screen) combines how much money active funds put into a stock, how much price impact that money has, and how many funds are buying. It favors small and mid caps, and when JPMorgan, BlackRock, Fidelity and T. Rowe all buy the same stock in the same week, that's a follow signal, not a fade.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: A legal 'smart money' signal for stock selection in small and mid caps where active buying moves prices; a Blue Horseshoe ETF has been discussed with a party in China.
insights.quote: Blue Horseshoe is as close as you can get I think to good information that isn't illegal.

insights.claim: Active equity ETF managers at JPMorgan and T. Rowe Price love the current environment because stock dispersion is through the roof, which makes it a genuine stock-picker's market.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: High dispersion favors active stock-picking and option sellers; expect continued active ETF asset growth.

insights.claim: Bitcoin is in a roughly 70% drawdown. A non-finance friend texting that his Bitcoin 'feels pretty dead' was read as a contrarian sign that the bottom is near.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Apathy among casual holders is a classic late-bear sentiment signal.
insights.quote: what should I do with my Bitcoin? It feels pretty dead. And I said, yeah, that's good news.

insights.claim: Eric Balchunas argues spot Bitcoin ETFs solved the intermediary problem: Bitcoin itself has never been hacked and the scams were always at exchanges and intermediaries, so ETFs are now the safest and cheapest access, making Bitcoin 'a tool at the adult table'.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: ETF access removes custody risk as a reason not to own Bitcoin and makes it a legitimate allocation question for advisers.
insights.quote: Bitcoin has never been hacked. It's never had a problem. It's always the intermediaries that are the scammy

insights.claim: Eric sees the next Bitcoin catalyst as government money printing, either a COVID-style crisis response (about $4 trillion) or reminders like Scott Bessent's Treasury buybacks, which set off a Bitcoin rally. He sees a dug-in true-believer base around $50,000-60,000.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: Watch for liquidity and debasement events as Bitcoin entry signals; $50-60K is the support zone the believers are defending.
insights.quote: I would look for anytime the government reminds us that they're just going to like print a lot of money.

insights.claim: A host's counterview: price itself is the catalyst. Bitcoin returning to $80,000, driven by Fed easing or a stock rally, would bring buyers back because momentum attracts speculators, and if Bitcoin rallies $10,000 it is more likely to rally another $10,000.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Treat Bitcoin as a momentum asset: trend confirmation, not the fundamental story, drives the next leg.
insights.quote: price is the catalyst.

insights.claim: A host argues legalized sports betting is crypto's real competitor, since Bitcoin is pure speculation with still no use cases 19 years in, and says many former Bitcoin true believers 'are all AI guys now'.
insights.speaker: host (Compound & Friends)
insights.so_what: Speculative capital moves between crypto, sports betting and AI themes; crypto demand is cyclical and competes for the same retail risk budget.
insights.quote: the problem for crypto >> was the legalization of sports betting.

insights.claim: About 50 million Americans own Bitcoin, twice as many as own an ETF, and the network has survived seven 50% drawdowns over 17 years with no boss. Guests argue the ETFs cleaned up the industry's scammer image, and that Bitcoin matters in countries with 50% inflation and asset seizures.
insights.speaker: James Seyffart and Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: The broad ownership base and history of recoveries argue against writing Bitcoin off in drawdowns.
insights.quote: Something that has survived seven 50% draw downs.

insights.claim: In 'Both Sides of the Coin', Barry Ritholtz calls the dollar purchasing-power chart 'the most misleading chart in all of finance' because wages rose too. The core debate is whether money should be a store of value or whether savers must invest their paycheck in assets immediately.
insights.speaker: Eric Balchunas
insights.so_what: The debasement case for Bitcoin depends on how you frame purchasing power; weigh the counter-argument before sizing a position.
insights.quote: he called that purchasing power chart the most misleading chart in all of finance.
